claim: Bacteria responsible for the greatest global mortality colonize the human microbiota far more frequently than they cause severe infections.
source: Bacteria responsible for the greatest global mortality colonize the human microbiota far more frequently than they cause severe infections.
evidence: Supported by citation to GBD 2015 study and established scientific knowledge about commensal bacteria.

claim: 72% of infections emerged from the nose.
source: We report that 72% of infections emerged from the nose, with infecting and nose-colonizing bacteria showing parallel adaptive differences.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 105 patients showing 76/105 patients had nose-ancestral infections.

claim: There is a 2.8-to-3.6-fold adaptive enrichment of protein-altering variants in genes responding to rsp.
source: We found 2.8-to-3.6-fold adaptive enrichments of protein-altering variants in genes responding to rsp, which regulates surface antigens and toxin production
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: rsp regulates surface antigens and toxin production.
source: rsp, which regulates surface antigens and toxin production
evidence: Supported by citation to Lei et al., 2011 and established knowledge about rsp function.

claim: agr regulates quorum-sensing, toxin production and abscess formation.
source: agr, which regulates quorum-sensing, toxin production and abscess formation
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about agr function.

claim: Adaptive mutations in pathogenesis-associated genes were 3.1-fold enriched in infecting but not nose-colonizing bacteria.
source: Adaptive mutations in pathogenesis-associated genes were 3.1-fold enriched in infecting but not nose-colonizing bacteria.
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data showing differential enrichment between BD-class and BC-class variants.

claim: The adaptive signatures were not observed in healthy carriers.
source: None of these signatures were observed in healthy carriers nor at the species-level, suggesting infection-associated, short-term, within-host selection pressures.
evidence: Supported by comparison to Reference Panel I (asymptomatic carriers) showing no significant enrichments.

claim: The adaptive signatures were not observed at the species-level.
source: None of these signatures were observed in healthy carriers nor at the species-level, suggesting infection-associated, short-term, within-host selection pressures.
evidence: Supported by dN/dS analysis between unrelated S. aureus showing no excess protein-altering change.

claim: 105 patients suffering severe S. aureus infections were identified with contemporaneous nose swabs.
source: We identified 105 patients suffering severe S. aureus infections admitted to hospitals in Oxford and Brighton, England, for whom we could recover contemporaneous nose swabs from admission screening.
evidence: Supported by study design and patient recruitment data.

claim: 55 patients had bloodstream infections.
source: Of the 105 patients, 55 had bloodstream infections, 37 had soft tissue infections and 13 had bone and joint infections (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by patient classification data in Table 1.

claim: 37 patients had soft tissue infections.
source: Of the 105 patients, 55 had bloodstream infections, 37 had soft tissue infections and 13 had bone and joint infections (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by patient classification data in Table 1.

claim: 13 patients had bone and joint infections.
source: Of the 105 patients, 55 had bloodstream infections, 37 had soft tissue infections and 13 had bone and joint infections (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by patient classification data in Table 1.

claim: 1163 bacterial colonies were whole-genome sequenced.
source: To discover de novo mutations within and between S. aureus in the nose and infection site, we whole-genome sequenced 1163 bacterial colonies, a median of 5 per site.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data from the study.

claim: A median of 5 colonies per site were sequenced.
source: To discover de novo mutations within and between S. aureus in the nose and infection site, we whole-genome sequenced 1163 bacterial colonies, a median of 5 per site.
evidence: Supported by sequencing methodology data.

claim: 35 distinct strains were identified across patients.
source: We identified 35 distinct strains, defined by multilocus sequence type (ST), across patients (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by MLST typing data.

claim: 95 patients possessed extremely closely related nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria, sharing the same ST and differing by 0–66 variants.
source: As expected (von Eiff et al., 2001), most patients possessed extremely closely related nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria, sharing the same ST and differing by 0–66 variants (95 patients).
evidence: Supported by genomic comparison data and citation to von Eiff et al., 2001.

claim: The nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria of nine patients were unrelated, possessing different STs and differing by 9398–50573 variants.
source: The nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria of nine patients were unrelated, possessing different STs and differing by 9398–50573 variants (e.g. Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by genomic comparison data and Figure 1A.

claim: 1322 de novo mutations arose within the 105 patients.
source: After excluding variants differentiating unrelated nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria, we catalogued 1322 de novo mutations that we deemed arose within the 105 patients.
evidence: Supported by variant calling and filtering data.

claim: Infecting and nose-colonizing bacteria usually formed closely related but distinct populations with no shared genotypes in 74/95 patients.
source: Infecting and nose-colonizing bacteria usually formed closely related but distinct populations with no shared genotypes (74/95 patients, e.g. Figure 1B), separated by a mean of 5.7 variants.
evidence: Supported by population structure analysis data and Figure 1B.

claim: Closely related populations were separated by a mean of 5.7 variants.
source: Infecting and nose-colonizing bacteria usually formed closely related but distinct populations with no shared genotypes (74/95 patients, e.g. Figure 1B), separated by a mean of 5.7 variants.
evidence: Supported by genetic distance calculations.

claim: There was never more than one identical genotype between nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria.
source: There was never more than one identical genotype between nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria, (21/95 patients, e.g. Figure 1C), indicating that the migration event from one population to the other involved a small number of founding bacteria (Moxon and Murphy, 1978; Margolis and Levin, 2007; Prajsnar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by genotype sharing analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: The migration event from one population to the other involved a small number of founding bacteria.
source: There was never more than one identical genotype between nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria, (21/95 patients, e.g. Figure 1C), indicating that the migration event from one population to the other involved a small number of founding bacteria (Moxon and Murphy, 1978; Margolis and Levin, 2007; Prajsnar et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from genotype sharing patterns and supported by citations.

claim: Genetic diversity in the nose (mean pairwise distance, π = 2.8 variants) was similar to that previously observed in asymptomatic nasal carriers (Reference Panel I, π = 4.1, p=0.13).
source: Genetic diversity in the nose (mean pairwise distance, π = 2.8 variants) was similar to that previously observed in asymptomatic nasal carriers (Golubchik et al., 2013) (Reference Panel I, π = 4.1, p=0.13)
evidence: Supported by comparison of genetic diversity metrics with citation to Golubchik et al., 2013.

claim: Genetic diversity was significantly lower in the infection site (π = 0.6, p=10–10.0).
source: but was significantly lower in the infection site (π = 0.6, p=10–10.0), revealing limited diversification post-infection.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of genetic diversity metrics.

claim: Limited diversification occurred post-infection.
source: but was significantly lower in the infection site (π = 0.6, p=10–10.0), revealing limited diversification post-infection.
evidence: Inferred from low genetic diversity in infection sites.

claim: The nose population was likely ancestral in 39/49 patients (80% of patients with related strains, or 72% of all patients).
source: The nose population was likely ancestral in 39/49 (80% of patients with related strains, or 72% of all patients) because all infecting bacteria shared de novo mutations in common that distinguished them from the MRCA, whereas nose-colonizing bacteria did not.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic reconstruction and MRCA analysis.

claim: In 10/49 patients, bacteria colonizing the nose were likely descended from blood or deep tissue infections (20% of patients with related strains, or 18% of all patients).
source: Conversely, in 10/49 patients, bacteria colonizing the nose were likely descended from blood or deep tissue infections (20% of patients with related strains, or 18% of all patients) (e.g. Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic reconstruction showing infection-ancestral populations.

claim: In persistent infections, infecting bacteria can recolonize the nose.
source: Confidence was high for just three of those patients, and they showed unusually high diversity (Supplementary data, P063, P072, P093), suggesting that in persistent infections, infecting bacteria can recolonize the nose.
evidence: Inferred from high diversity in infection-ancestral cases.

claim: The prevailing tendency of selection within patients was to conserve protein sequences, with dN/dS ratios of 0.55, 0.68 and 0.63 for B-, C- and D-class variants, respectively.
source: As expected, the prevailing tendency of selection within patients was to conserve protein sequences, with dN/dS ratios indicating rates of non-synonymous change 0.55, 0.68 and 0.63 times the rate expected under strict neutral evolution for B-, C- and D-class variants, respectively.
evidence: Supported by dN/dS ratio calculations from variant data.

claim: There is a 3.9-fold over-abundance of protein-truncating variants in infected patients compared to asymptomatic carriers (p=0.002).
source: Here, we found a 3.9-fold over-abundance of protein-truncating variants of all phylogenetic classes in infected patients compared to asymptomatic carriers (Reference Panel I, p=0.002, Table 2)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison with Reference Panel I data in Table 2.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations are disproportionately associated with evolution within infected patients.
source: supporting the conclusion that loss-of-function mutations are disproportionately associated with evolution within infected patients.
evidence: Inferred from enrichment of protein-truncating variants in infected patients.

claim: agrA showed a significant excess of five protein-altering B-class variants representing a 58.3-fold enrichment (p=10–7.5).
source: We found a significant excess of five protein-altering B-class variants representing a 58.3-fold enrichment in agrA, which encodes the response regulator that mediates activation of the quorum-sensing system at high cell densities (p=10–7.5, Figure 2A, Table 3).
evidence: Supported by gene enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 2A and Table 3.

claim: agrA encodes the response regulator that mediates activation of the quorum-sensing system at high cell densities.
source: agrA, which encodes the response regulator that mediates activation of the quorum-sensing system at high cell densities
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about agrA function.

claim: clfB showed an excess of five protein-altering B-class variants, representing a 15.9-fold enrichment that was near genome-wide significance (p=10–4.7).
source: The clfB gene encoding clumping factor B, which binds human fibrinogen and loricrin (Foster et al., 2013), showed an excess of five protein-altering B-class variants, representing a 15.9-fold enrichment that was near genome-wide significance after multiple testing correction (p=10–4.7).
evidence: Supported by gene enrichment analysis data and citation to Foster et al., 2013.

claim: Clumping factor B binds human fibrinogen and loricrin.
source: The clfB gene encoding clumping factor B, which binds human fibrinogen and loricrin (Foster et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Foster et al., 2013.

claim: pbp2 showed a significant excess of six protein-altering C-class variants (19.0-fold enrichment, p=10–6.0).
source: We found no significant enrichments of protein-altering variants among D-class variants, but we observed a significant excess of six protein-altering C-class variants in pbp2 which encodes a penicillin binding protein involved in cell wall synthesis (19.0-fold enrichment, p=10–6.0, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by gene enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pbp2 encodes a penicillin binding protein involved in cell wall synthesis.
source: pbp2 which encodes a penicillin binding protein involved in cell wall synthesis
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about pbp2 function.

claim: Pbp2 is an important target of β-lactam antibiotics.
source: Pbp2 is an important target of β-lactam antibiotics (Łeski and Tomasz, 2005), revealing adaption – potentially in response to antibiotic treatment – in the nose populations of some patients.
evidence: Supported by citation to Łeski and Tomasz, 2005.

claim: Adaptation potentially in response to antibiotic treatment occurred in the nose populations of some patients.
source: Pbp2 is an important target of β-lactam antibiotics (Łeski and Tomasz, 2005), revealing adaption – potentially in response to antibiotic treatment – in the nose populations of some patients.
evidence: Inferred from enrichment of pbp2 variants in nose-colonizing bacteria.

claim: The most significant enrichment for protein-altering B-class variants occurred in genes down-regulated by the cationic antimicrobial peptide ovispirin-1 (p=10–7.8).
source: The most significant enrichment for protein-altering B-class variants between nose and infection sites occurred in the group of genes down-regulated by the cationic antimicrobial peptide (CAMP) ovispirin-1 (p=10–7.8)
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data.

claim: There was a similar enrichment in genes down-regulated by temporin L exposure (p=10–6.9).
source: with a similar enrichment in genes down-regulated by temporin L exposure (p=10–6.9, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ovispirin and temporin compounds inhibit epithelial infections by killing phagocytosed bacteria and mediating inflammatory responses.
source: Like human CAMPs, the animal-derived ovispirin and temporin compounds inhibit epithelial infections by killing phagocytosed bacteria and mediating inflammatory responses (Pietiäinen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pietiäinen et al., 2009.

claim: In response to inhibitory levels of ovispirin and temporin, agr, surface-expressed adhesins and secreted toxins are all down-regulated.
source: In response to inhibitory levels of ovispirin and temporin, agr, surface-expressed adhesins and secreted toxins are all down-regulated.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pietiäinen et al., 2009.

claim: Genes down-regulated by ovispirin showed 2.7-fold enrichment of adaptive evolution.
source: Collectively, down-regulated genes showed 2.7-fold and 2.8-fold enrichments of adaptive evolution, respectively.
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis calculations.

claim: Genes down-regulated by temporin showed 2.8-fold enrichment of adaptive evolution.
source: Collectively, down-regulated genes showed 2.7-fold and 2.8-fold enrichments of adaptive evolution, respectively.
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis calculations.

claim: Genes up-regulated in response to CAMPs exhibited 0.4-fold and 0.7-fold enrichments (i.e. depletions).
source: Conversely, genes up-regulated in response to CAMPs, including the vraSR and vraDE cell-wall operons and stress response genes (Pietiäinen et al., 2009), exhibited 0.4-fold and 0.7-fold enrichments (i.e. depletions), respectively (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data in Table 3 and citation to Pietiäinen et al., 2009.

claim: Expression of the genes undergoing adaptive evolution is strongly inhibited in vitro by host-derived antimicrobial peptides.
source: Thus, expression of the genes undergoing adaptive evolution is strongly inhibited in vitro by host-derived antimicrobial peptides.
evidence: Inferred from enrichment patterns in CAMP-regulated genes.

claim: Genes belonging to the cell wall ontology showed a 5.0-fold enrichment for adaptive evolution (p=10–7.0).
source: Genes belonging to the cell wall ontology showed the second most significant enrichment for adaptive evolution (p=10–7.0).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data.

claim: There is a 6.4-fold enrichment of adaptive protein evolution in the cell adhesion ontology (p=10–6.5).
source: The latter four genes contributed to another statistically significant 6.4-fold enrichment of adaptive protein evolution in the cell adhesion ontology (p=10–6.5, Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is a general enrichment of surface-expressed host-binding antigens undergoing adaptive evolution.
source: Therefore, there is a general enrichment of surface-expressed host-binding antigens undergoing adaptive evolution.
evidence: Inferred from enrichments in cell wall and cell adhesion ontologies.

claim: The rsp regulon showed the most significant enrichment among gene sets defined by response to individual bacterial regulators (p=10–6.4).
source: The rsp regulon showed the most significant enrichment among gene sets defined by response to individual bacterial regulators (p=10–6.4).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data.

claim: Genes down-regulated by rsp in exponential phase exhibited a 3.6-fold enrichment for adaptive evolution.
source: Genes down-regulated by rsp in exponential phase (Lei et al., 2011), including surface antigens and the urease operon, exhibited a 3.6-fold enrichment for adaptive evolution, while up-regulated genes showed 0.6-fold enrichment.
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data and citation to Lei et al., 2011.

claim: Genes up-regulated by rsp showed 0.6-fold enrichment.
source: Genes down-regulated by rsp in exponential phase (Lei et al., 2011), including surface antigens and the urease operon, exhibited a 3.6-fold enrichment for adaptive evolution, while up-regulated genes showed 0.6-fold enrichment.
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data.

claim: There are alternative routes by which genes down-regulated by intact rsp can be expressed and play an important role within patients other than direct inactivation of rsp.
source: Since expression is a prerequisite for adaptive protein evolution, this implies there are alternative routes by which genes down-regulated by intact rsp can be expressed and thereby play an important role within patients other than direct inactivation of rsp.
evidence: Inferred from enrichment of rsp-regulated genes despite rarity of rsp mutations.

claim: agr loss-of-function mutants exhibit similar phenotypes to rsp mutants, with reduced cytotoxicity and increased surface antigen expression.
source: Loss-of-function in agr mutants represent one alternative route, since they exhibit similar phenotypes to rsp mutants, with reduced cytotoxicity and increased surface antigen expression, albeit reduced ability to form abscesses (Das et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Das et al., 2016.

claim: agr loss-of-function mutants have reduced ability to form abscesses.
source: Loss-of-function in agr mutants represent one alternative route, since they exhibit similar phenotypes to rsp mutants, with reduced cytotoxicity and increased surface antigen expression, albeit reduced ability to form abscesses (Das et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Das et al., 2016.

claim: Significant enrichments of genes regulated by agrA were found in two different backgrounds (p<10–4.5).
source: We found significant enrichments of genes regulated by agrA in two different backgrounds (p<10–4.5) and by sarA (p=10–4.6)
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data.

claim: Significant enrichments of genes regulated by sarA were found (p=10–4.6).
source: We found significant enrichments of genes regulated by agrA in two different backgrounds (p<10–4.5) and by sarA (p=10–4.6)
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data.

claim: Expression of genes enriched for protein-altering substitutions was altered in strains possessing reduced susceptibility to vancomycin (p<10–4.7).
source: We found that expression of genes enriched for protein-altering substitutions was also altered in strains possessing reduced susceptibility to vancomycin, although not in a consistent direction across strains (p<10–4.7)
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data.

claim: Expression of genes enriched for protein-altering substitutions was altered in strains with reduced susceptibility to pine-oil disinfectant (p=10–4.4).
source: and to pine-oil disinfectant (p=10–4.4), suggesting such genes may be generally involved in response to harsh environments.
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data.

claim: Genes enriched for protein-altering substitutions may be generally involved in response to harsh environments.
source: and to pine-oil disinfectant (p=10–4.4), suggesting such genes may be generally involved in response to harsh environments.
evidence: Speculative inference from enrichment patterns in stress-related conditions.

claim: All significant signals of enrichment produced neutrality indices exceeding one, consistent with adaptive evolution.
source: All significant signals of enrichment produced neutrality indices exceeding one, consistent with adaptive evolution (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by neutrality index calculations.

claim: Genes belonging to the BioCyc pathogenesis ontology showed a 3.1-fold enrichment in BD-class variants (p=10–4.6).
source: Genes belonging to the BioCyc pathogenesis ontology were marginally genome-wide significant in BD-class variants, showing a 3.1-fold enrichment (p=10–4.6) and a statistically insignificant 1.7-fold enrichment in BC-class variants (p=0.13).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data comparing BC-class and BD-class variants.

claim: Genes belonging to the BioCyc pathogenesis ontology showed a statistically insignificant 1.7-fold enrichment in BC-class variants (p=0.13).
source: Genes belonging to the BioCyc pathogenesis ontology were marginally genome-wide significant in BD-class variants, showing a 3.1-fold enrichment (p=10–4.6) and a statistically insignificant 1.7-fold enrichment in BC-class variants (p=0.13).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis data.

claim: Adaptation in pathogenesis genes appears specifically infection-associated.
source: So while adaptation in pathogenesis genes appears specifically infection-associated, other signals of adaptation in severely infected patients are driven by selection pressures, which might compensate for an altered within-host environment during infection, that are as likely to favor mutants in nose-colonizing bacteria as infecting bacteria.
evidence: Inferred from differential enrichment of pathogenesis genes in BD-class vs BC-class variants.

claim: Other signals of adaptation in severely infected patients are driven by selection pressures that are as likely to favor mutants in nose-colonizing bacteria as infecting bacteria.
source: So while adaptation in pathogenesis genes appears specifically infection-associated, other signals of adaptation in severely infected patients are driven by selection pressures, which might compensate for an altered within-host environment during infection, that are as likely to favor mutants in nose-colonizing bacteria as infecting bacteria.
evidence: Inferred from similar enrichments in BC-class and BD-class variants for most gene sets.

claim: There was no significant enrichment of protein-altering variants in any gene, ontology or pathway among 235 variants identified from 10 longitudinally sampled asymptomatic nasal carriers.
source: There was no significant enrichment of protein-altering variants in any gene, ontology or pathway among 235 variants identified from 10 longitudinally sampled asymptomatic nasal carriers (Reference Panel III, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis of Reference Panel III data.

claim: There were significant depletions of protein-altering variants in carriers relative to patients in the rsp, agr and sarA regulons (p=10–4.0).
source: We found significant depletions of protein-altering variants in carriers relative to patients in the rsp, agr and sarA regulons (p=10–4.0) and the pathogenesis ontology (p=10–3.2, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by goodness-of-fit tests comparing carriers to patients.

claim: There were significant depletions of protein-altering variants in carriers relative to patients in the pathogenesis ontology (p=10–3.2).
source: We found significant depletions of protein-altering variants in carriers relative to patients in the rsp, agr and sarA regulons (p=10–4.0) and the pathogenesis ontology (p=10–3.2, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by goodness-of-fit tests comparing carriers to patients.

claim: The dN/dS ratios showed no evidence for excess protein-altering change in agrA, agrC, clfA, clfB, fnbA and sasA compared to other genes.
source: Although synonymous diversity was somewhat higher than typical in these genes, the dN/dS ratios showed no evidence for excess protein-altering change in these compared to other genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by dN/dS analysis between unrelated S. aureus shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ontologies, pathways and genes significantly differentiated between nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria arise in response to selection pressures specifically associated with infected patients.
source: Taken together these lines of evidence show that the ontologies, pathways and genes significantly differentiated between nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria arise in response to selection pressures specifically associated with infected patients, and are not repeated in asymptomatic carriers or species-level evolution.
evidence: Inferred from comparisons with asymptomatic carriers and species-level evolution.

claim: The signatures of within-patient adaptation are not repeated in asymptomatic carriers or species-level evolution.
source: Taken together these lines of evidence show that the ontologies, pathways and genes significantly differentiated between nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria arise in response to selection pressures specifically associated with infected patients, and are not repeated in asymptomatic carriers or species-level evolution.
evidence: Supported by comparisons with Reference Panels III and IV.

claim: Common, life-threatening infections of S. aureus are frequently descended from commensal bacteria colonizing the nose.
source: We found that common, life-threatening infections of S. aureus are frequently descended from commensal bacteria colonizing the nose.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis showing 72% of infections emerged from the nose.

claim: These infections are associated with repeatable patterns of bacterial evolution driven by within-patient mutation and selection.
source: These infections are associated with repeatable patterns of bacterial evolution driven by within-patient mutation and selection.
evidence: Supported by enrichment analyses showing parallel adaptive evolution across patients.

claim: Genes involved in pathogenesis, notably toxins and regulators, showed evidence for adaptation in infecting but not nose-colonizing bacteria.
source: Genes involved in pathogenesis, notably toxins and regulators, showed evidence for adaptation in infecting but not nose-colonizing bacteria.
evidence: Supported by differential enrichment in BD-class vs BC-class variants.

claim: Other signatures of adaptation occurred in parallel in nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria, affecting genes responding to cationic antimicrobial peptides and the virulence regulators rsp and agr.
source: Surprisingly, other signatures of adaptation occurred in parallel in nose-colonizing and infecting bacteria, affecting genes responding to cationic antimicrobial peptides and the virulence regulators rsp and agr.
evidence: Supported by enrichment analyses showing similar patterns in BC-class and BD-class variants.

claim: Such genes mediate toxin production, abscess formation, immune evasion and bacterial-host binding.
source: Such genes mediate toxin production, abscess formation, immune evasion and bacterial-host binding.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology and functional annotations.

claim: Adaptation within both regulator and effector genes reveals that multiple, alternative evolutionary paths are targeted by selection in infected patients.
source: Adaptation within both regulator and effector genes reveals that multiple, alternative evolutionary paths are targeted by selection in infected patients.
evidence: Inferred from enrichments in both regulatory genes and their targets.

claim: The signatures of within-patient adaptation differed from prevailing signals of selection at the species level.
source: The signatures of within-patient adaptation that we found differed from prevailing signals of selection at the species level.
evidence: Supported by comparison of within-patient enrichments to species-level dN/dS ratios.

claim: Infection-associated adaptive mutations within patients are rarely transmitted.
source: This discordance means that infection-associated adaptive mutations within patients are rarely transmitted, and argues against a straightforward host-pathogen arms race as the predominant evolutionary force acting within and between patients.
evidence: Inferred from discordance between within-patient and species-level selection signatures.

claim: The discordance argues against a straightforward host-pathogen arms race as the predominant evolutionary force acting within and between patients.
source: This discordance means that infection-associated adaptive mutations within patients are rarely transmitted, and argues against a straightforward host-pathogen arms race as the predominant evolutionary force acting within and between patients.
evidence: Inferred from lack of transmission of infection-associated mutations.

claim: The findings support the notion of a life-history trade-off between adaptations favoring colonization and infection distinct from those favoring dissemination and onward transmission.
source: Instead, it supports the notion of a life-history trade-off between adaptations favoring colonization and infection distinct from those favoring dissemination and onward transmission (Shopsin et al., 2010).
evidence: Inferred from discordance between within-patient and species-level selection, supported by citation to Shopsin et al., 2010.

claim: Infection can be characterized in terms of an ecological source-sink model, in which commensal bacteria provide the source for potentially life-threatening infections.
source: Infection of this sort can be characterized in terms of an ecological source-sink model, in which commensal bacteria provide the source for potentially life-threatening infections (Sokurenko et al., 2006).
evidence: Theoretical interpretation supported by citation to Sokurenko et al., 2006.

claim: Infection may represent an ever-present risk of mutation among commensal bacteria favored by short-term selection but ultimately incidental or damaging to the bacterial reproductive life cycle.
source: As such, infection may represent an ever-present risk of mutation among commensal bacteria favored by short-term selection but ultimately incidental or damaging to the bacterial reproductive life cycle.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the evolutionary dynamics observed.

claim: Risk factors for infections may play an important role in creating distinctive selection pressures in infected patients.
source: We did not observe analogous signatures of bacterial adaptation and excess loss-of-function mutations in healthy nose carriers, indicating that risk factors for infections, such as a weakened or over-activated immunological response, comorbidities or medical interventions, may play an important role in creating distinctive selection pressures in infected patients.
evidence: Inferred from absence of adaptive signatures in healthy carriers.

claim: The effects of risk factors may be mediated, at least in part, through the selection pressure they exert on commensal bacteria.
source: The effects of such risk factors may be mediated, at least in part, through the selection pressure they exert on commensal bacteria.
evidence: Speculative inference about mechanism of risk factor effects.

claim: The existence of signatures of adaptive substitutions associated with infection raises the possibility of developing new diagnostic techniques.
source: The existence of signatures of adaptive substitutions associated with infection raises the possibility of developing new diagnostic techniques and personalizing treatment to the individual patient's commensal bacteria.
evidence: Speculative implication of the findings.

claim: The existence of signatures of adaptive substitutions associated with infection raises the possibility of personalizing treatment to the individual patient's commensal bacteria.
source: The existence of signatures of adaptive substitutions associated with infection raises the possibility of developing new diagnostic techniques and personalizing treatment to the individual patient's commensal bacteria.
evidence: Speculative implication of the findings.

claim: Genomics provides new opportunities to improve experimental models of infection.
source: The ability of genomics to characterize the selective forces driving adaption within the human body in unprecedented detail provides new opportunities to improve experimental models of infection.
evidence: Speculative implication of genomic approaches.

claim: It may be possible to develop therapies that utilize understanding of within-patient evolution to target the root causes of infection from the bacterial perspective.
source: Ultimately, it may be possible to develop therapies that utilize our new understanding of within-patient evolution to target the root causes of infection from the bacterial perspective.
evidence: Speculative future application of the findings.

claim: Many bacteria imposing the greatest burden of mortality are frequently found as commensal components of the body's microbiota.
source: However, many of the bacteria imposing the greatest burden of mortality, such as Staphylococcus aureus, are frequently found as commensal components of the body's microbiota (Turnbaugh et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Turnbaugh et al., 2007 and established knowledge.

claim: For commensal bacteria, infection is a relatively uncommon event that is often unnecessary for onward transmission.
source: For them, infection is a relatively uncommon event that is often unnecessary (Casadevall et al., 2011; Méthot and Alizon, 2014), and perhaps disadvantageous (Brown et al., 2012), for onward transmission.
evidence: Supported by citations to Casadevall et al., 2011; Méthot and Alizon, 2014; Brown et al., 2012.

claim: Infection may be disadvantageous for onward transmission.
source: For them, infection is a relatively uncommon event that is often unnecessary (Casadevall et al., 2011; Méthot and Alizon, 2014), and perhaps disadvantageous (Brown et al., 2012), for onward transmission.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2012.

claim: Common bacterial infections, including S. aureus, are often associated with colonization of the nose by a genetically similar strain.
source: Common bacterial infections, including S. aureus, are often associated with colonization of the nose by a genetically similar strain.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and subsequent citations.

claim: In patients with S. aureus infections, the nose is considered the likely source of infection because the nose is more often the site of asymptomatic colonization than any other body site.

claim: Five colonies per sample is expected to confer 91% power to correctly distinguish within-site polymorphisms from between-site substitutions.
